name: Lima
info: Lima is the capital of Peru, on the desert coast in the valleys of the Chillón, Rímac and Lurín rivers; Francisco Pizarro founded it in 1535, and it became the capital of the Viceroyalty of Peru and then of the republic.

facts.founded: Francisco Pizarro founded the city in 1535 as the City of Kings, on land that had belonged to the local lord Taulichusco, in a valley long held by the Ichma polity.
facts.where: In the valleys of the Chillón, Rímac and Lurín rivers on the desert coast of central Peru, overlooking the Pacific Ocean, with the port of Callao beside it.
facts.known: The Spanish City of Kings; capital of the Viceroyalty of Peru; the silver trade through Callao; the earthquake of 1687; the oldest continuously operating university of the New World; the Lord of Miracles procession; the Historic Centre
facts.today: Lima is the capital and largest city of Peru, with about 10 million inhabitants, and its historic centre is a World Heritage Site.

t: Pizarro founded Lima in 1535 in a valley that the Ichma, the Wari and then the Inca had held, and in 1543 it became the capital of the Viceroyalty of Peru.
It grew rich in the 17th century on the silver trade through Callao, then lost ground to earthquakes, new viceroyalties and the Bourbon Reforms, and in 1821 it became the capital of independent Peru.
Migration from the Andes from the 1940s made it one of the largest cities of South America, and it is now the capital of Peru, holding about a third of the country's people in its metropolitan area.
dyk: The name Lima probably comes from Limaq, the name of a famous oracle in the Rímac valley that the Spanish destroyed and replaced with a church.
ev: Francisco Pizarro founds the City of Kings in the Rímac valley
Troops sent by Manco Inca besiege the city and are defeated by the Spanish and their indigenous allies
Lima becomes the capital of the Viceroyalty of Peru and the seat of a Real Audiencia
Earthquakes on 20 October and 2 December destroy most of the city
An earthquake severely damages Lima and destroys Callao
The viceroy leaves, and the city council signs a Declaration of Independence at the request of San Martín
The War of the Pacific begins, and Chilean troops later occupy and loot the city
An earthquake strikes, and rapid growth from migration from the Andes begins

sections.origins:
Lima lies on the desert coast of central Peru, in the valleys of the Chillón, Rímac and Lurín rivers, overlooking the Pacific Ocean. The city began with its Spanish foundation in 1535, but the valleys were occupied long before. Pre-Inca settlements there were grouped under the Lordship of Ichma, and the Maranga and Lima cultures established an identity in these territories. The Wari Empire conquered these cultures, and the ceremonial centre of Cajamarquilla was built during that time. As Wari importance declined, local cultures regained autonomy, notably the Chancay culture, and in the 15th century the territory was incorporated into the Inca Empire. The Ichma left some 40 pyramids tied to the irrigation system of the valleys.

Before the Spanish arrived, a famous oracle in the Rímac valley was known as Limaq, which means "talker" or "speaker" in the coastal Quechua that was the area's main language. The Spanish destroyed the oracle and replaced it with a church, but the name persisted, and scholars think "Lima" is the Spanish pronunciation of Limaq. In Inca times the valley was highly populated and formed a province called Pachacamac. The part of it near the Rímac was administered by a local lord, a curaca named Taulichusco, who had been awarded it for his services to the Inca royalty. His residential palace stood where the Government Palace stands today.
sections.growth:
Lima rose quickly after its foundation. In 1541 it became the seat of a Roman Catholic diocese, in 1543 the capital of the Viceroyalty of Peru, and in 1551 it gained the National University of San Marcos. Its first printing press followed in 1584. The city flourished in the 17th century as the centre of a trade network that joined the viceroyalty with the Americas, Europe and the Far East. Its merchants sent Peruvian silver through the nearby port of Callao and exchanged it for imported goods at the trade fair of Portobelo in modern Panama, and law required all the viceroyalty's overseas trade to pass through Callao. The population grew from about 25,000 in 1619 to an estimated 80,000 in 1687.

The decline came after 1687, when an earthquake coincided with a recession in trade, a fall in silver production and competition from cities such as Buenos Aires. In the second half of the 18th century the Bourbon Reforms took away the city's monopoly on overseas trade, and the mining region of Upper Peru passed to the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata. Revenue from guano exports revived growth in the 1850s, and the state paid for large public buildings such as the Central Market and the Hospital Dos de Mayo. A railway to Callao was completed in 1850, and the iron Balta Bridge opened in 1870. The population passed 100,000 in 1861 and had doubled by 1927.
sections.rulers:
Before 1535 the valleys passed from the Lordship of Ichma to the Wari Empire, then back to local rule, and in the 15th century to the Inca Empire. In 1532 Francisco Pizarro and his Spanish and indigenous allies took the Inca ruler Atahualpa prisoner at Cajamarca. Atahualpa was sentenced to death although a ransom had been paid, and the Spanish went on to conquer his empire. The Spanish Crown named Pizarro governor of the lands he had conquered, and he founded Lima as his capital after a failed attempt to establish one at Jauja. In 1543 Lima became the capital of the Viceroyalty of Peru, and the viceroys governed from it. The creation of the Viceroyalty of New Granada in 1717 and of the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata in 1776 reduced the territory it governed.

In the 1810s the city was a Royalist stronghold under the viceroy José Fernando de Abascal y Sousa. A Patriot expedition under General José de San Martín landed south of Lima in 1820. Faced with a naval blockade and guerrilla action, the viceroy José de la Serna evacuated the city in July 1821, and San Martín proclaimed the independence of Peru. Lima became the seat of his government and of the first Constituent Congress, and the capital of the Republic of Peru. In the War of the Pacific (1879 to 1883) Chilean troops occupied the city after the battles of San Juan and Miraflores.
sections.life:
Pizarro, with Nicolás de Ribera, Diego de Agüero and Francisco Quintero, traced the Plaza Mayor and the street grid, and the first settlement had 117 housing blocks. In 1562 another district was built across the Rímac, and the first stone bridge dates from 1610. At that time Lima had about 26,000 people, of whom around 40 per cent were black and around 38 per cent white. The Afro-Peruvians of today descend from Africans first brought to the region as slaves. The city was the residence of Spanish nobles in large houses and palaces and of many religious orders, and in the 17th century it became a city of monastic life, home to Saint Rose of Lima and Saint Martín de Porres. The image of Christ called the Lord of Miracles has been carried in procession every October since 1746, and the city council named it patron of the city in 1715.

In the late 18th century Enlightenment ideas of public health led to a cockfighting coliseum, the Acho bullring and a General Cemetery, which ended burial in churches. Chinese and fewer Japanese immigrants arrived in the 19th and early 20th centuries and settled in Barrios Altos, and other immigrants founded their own schools. The Spanish of Lima was shaped by the Castilian nobility of the viceroyalty and later by Italian, African, Chinese, Japanese and Andean influences. The newspaper El Comercio was founded in 1839.
sections.crises:
In August 1536 the new city was besieged by troops sent by the Inca ruler Manco Inca, who was leading a rebellion against Spanish rule. After heavy fighting in the streets and around the city, the Spanish and their indigenous allies, among them the Huaylas army under Contarhuancho, defeated them. Earthquakes destroyed a large part of Lima between 1586 and 1687, and those of 20 October and 2 December 1687 destroyed most of the city. Disease and food shortages followed, and the population fell to under 40,000 by 1692. On 28 October 1746 another earthquake severely damaged the city and destroyed Callao, and Viceroy José Antonio Manso de Velasco directed the rebuilding.

Pirates and privateers also threatened Lima. A Dutch fleet under Jacques l'Hermite attacked Callao in 1624 and was repelled, English buccaneers were routed by Lima merchants in 1690, and the city walls were built between 1684 and 1687. During the wars of independence the city changed hands several times in two years and suffered exactions from both sides. In the War of the Pacific, after the battles of San Juan and Miraflores, Chilean troops looted museums, libraries and schools, and angry mobs attacked wealthy citizens and the Asian community and sacked their businesses. An earthquake struck on 24 May 1940, when most of the city was built of adobe and quincha. In the 1980s the Shining Path and the Túpac Amaru Revolutionary Movement were centred in Lima, and terrorist violence added to the displacement of people and the decay of the historic centre.
sections.legacy:
The Historic Centre of Lima was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1988. Its colonial buildings include the Basilica and Convent of San Francisco, the Metropolitan Cathedral and the Palacio de Torre Tagle, in styles drawn from Spanish Baroque and Neoclassicism, and it holds over 1,600 balconies from the viceregal and republican periods. Pre-Hispanic huacas such as Huallamarca, Pucllana and Mateo Salado still stand among the business and residential buildings of districts that have grown around them. The National University of San Marcos, founded in 1551, is the oldest continuously operating university in the New World, and the National Library of Peru was founded in 1821.

The rapid growth that began in the 1940s came from migration from the Andean regions. The population, estimated at 600,000 in 1940, reached 1.9 million by 1960 and 4.8 million by 1980. Migrants raised shanty towns known as barriadas, later called pueblos jóvenes, through large land invasions. Lima is now the capital and largest city of Peru. A 2023 census projection gives the city about 10 million people, and around a third of the country's population lives in its metropolitan area. Its cooking mixes Spanish, Andean, African, Chinese and Japanese traditions, from the immigrants and migrants who settled there.

summary: Lima, in the valleys of the Chillón, Rímac and Lurín rivers on the coast of Peru, was founded by Francisco Pizarro in 1535 in a valley long held by the Ichma, the Wari and the Inca. It became the capital of the Viceroyalty of Peru and then of the republic, and it is now a city of about 10 million people.
references: Kenneth J. Andrien, Crisis and Decline: The Viceroyalty of Peru in the Seventeenth Century (University of New Mexico Press, 1985)
Timothy E. Anna, The Fall of the Royal Government in Peru (University of Nebraska Press, 1979)
James Higgins, Lima: A Cultural History (Oxford University Press, 2005)
notes: FOUNDING DAY: History of Lima says 18 January 1535; Lima says 6 January 1535 (the feast of the Epiphany, the reason for the name City of Kings). I gave the year only.
ARCHDIOCESE: History says the diocese of 1541 became an archdiocese five years later (1546); Lima says 1547. I gave the diocese of 1541 only.

SIEGE OF 1536: History says troops of Manco Inca; Lima says troops of the Inca general Quizu Yupanqui under orders from Manco Inca. I wrote 'troops sent by Manco Inca'. Lima names Contarhuancho of Huaylas as leading allies; History does not.
SIEGE DATE vs ev: Pizarro 'ambushed' Atahualpa in History; Lima says took him prisoner at Cajamarca in 1532. I used Lima's wording and the year 1532 only in rulers.
CHILEAN OCCUPATION: the articles give no year for the occupation, only the war (1879-1883); the ev entry for 1879 is the war.

San Martin's landing: History gives 7 September 1820; Lima gives only 1820. I gave 1820. Independence proclaimed: I put 'San Martin proclaimed the independence of Peru' from Lima; the articles do not give a day.

EARTHQUAKES: Lima says violent earthquakes destroyed 'a large part' of the city between 1586 and 1687; History says the two of 1687 destroyed 'most of the city and its surroundings'. Both kept as written.
POPULATION: 25,000 (1619) to 80,000 (1687) from History; 26,000 about 1610 from Lima. Different years, both kept only partly (1610 figure in life).
QUINGNAM, Aymara, Pachacamac's hunu counts and Rowe's 150,000 are disputed or hedged in the article; left out. Cobo's 'three hunu' left out.

Present-day figure: Lima gives 10,092,000 for the city from a 2023 projection and 10,151,200 for the metropolitan area; I wrote 'about 10 million' without a year. 'Around a third' follows 'around one-third of the national population' in the metropolitan area; elsewhere the article says 29% and 36%.

Left out as tourism, sport, rankings, airports, transport, present government and economy: the Pan American Games, restaurants, Mistura, World's 50 Best, the 2022-2023 protests, the Metro, Chancay port.

'Lima is a Royalist stronghold in the 1810s under Abascal' is from History. The Dutch 1624 attack is dated, the 1690 rout is dated; the 'wars of independence ... changed hands several times in two years' is History's 'next two years'.
Saint Rose of Lima and Martín de Porres are named in the Religion section of Lima as saints of the 17th-century city; Martín de Porres is called a saint there without a date.
'Chinese and fewer Japanese ... 19th and early 20th centuries': the Demographics section says most came then; the Barrios Altos settlement is from the Settlement section.
Spanish of Lima: 'Castilian nobility' and the immigrant influences are from the Language section; I dropped the claim about clarity.
